dimensions.note: Neither report holds, receives or reads a credential. Both are read-only consumers of resource snapshots that other models already wrote, and the models that DO hold B2 credentials (b2-account, b2-files) are independently asserted never to write one into a snapshot. So the only way a secret could reach this package is if an upstream snapshot carried one, which their own suites forbid. The new workflow-scope report widens the read surface — it reads a second model's snapshots via stepExecutions — but not the sensitivity of what it reads: aggregate carries byte counts, file counts and timestamps, no identifiers beyond bucket names and IDs. Re-checked against the live output: the rendered markdown and JSON from two real fleet runs contain bucket names, bucket IDs and application key IDs (already masked as 002***0000000003 by b2-account upstream), and no token, key material or URL.

Both reports log one structured summary line with named placeholders and a props object, never string concatenation. The new report's line carries the fact a reader most needs and would otherwise have to compute — whether the byte total is a floor — as an explicit suffix rather than leaving it implied by a flag elsewhere. The markdown itself is the real output surface and it is ordered on a deliberate principle, inherited from the method-scope report and made stricter here: every incompleteness caveat renders ABOVE the number it qualifies, because a caveat printed below a total does not get read and a total quoted without its caveat is worse than no total. Asserted by test rather than by inspection ('the floor warning appears before any byte total' compares string indices).

Neither report can fail a workflow — swamp treats a throwing report as advisory — so the risk here is not crashing but returning something confidently wrong. Every read is defensive: readSnapshot returns null on both a missing blob and a JSON parse failure, and an unreadable snapshot is skipped rather than counted as a clean object (asserted in both suites). The refusal paths are explicit and tested: no succeeded step wrote an inventory, a failed inventory step, and a failed sizing step. The last is the sharpest and was designed against rather than discovered — a sizing step that died partway may well have written real aggregates, so totalling those and presenting them as the fleet would produce a confident under-count; the code requires status === 'succeeded' before reading a single aggregate, and 'a failed sizing step contributes no bytes at all' asserts the byte total never appears.

51 tests (22 existing + 29 new), and this dimension's previously-recorded ISSUE is now CLOSED: the prior review's only gap was that b2/hygiene had never run against live data, and the b2-fleet-audit workflow has now run end-to-end against the real account twice today, producing 52 findings over 24 buckets and 23 keys. Two defects were found in the process that no mock caught, and both are fixed and tested. (1) The 22 existing tests HAD NEVER RUN: `deno test` aborted at type-check because `execute` carried no declared return type, so TypeScript inferred a union with the early-return skip object and every `out.json.<field>` access failed to compile. They passed under --no-check, which is why it went unnoticed — a suite that cannot be executed is indistinguishable from a suite that is green if nobody reads the exit status. Fixed by declaring ReportResult and annotating both reports' execute; the 22 now genuinely run under type-check. (2) A live-only rendering defect, recorded under resource-management. The new suite was proven to bite by mutation rather than assumed: coercing the null-propagating sum to `?? 0` failed 'a null byte field makes the sum unknown rather than smaller'. A SECOND mutation — dropping the unmeasurable-bucket exclusion from the fleet total — initially passed all 29 tests, which exposed a genuine hole in my own coverage rather than a false alarm; the test now asserts currentBytes as well, and the mutation fails. Both mutations were reverted and the suite re-verified green.

Both reports are pure functions of already-written snapshots: they call no API, mutate nothing, and re-running one over the same data produces the same output. Verified rather than assumed — the workflow ran twice today over an unchanged fleet and the second run reproduced the first's finding count (52), bucket count (24) and byte total (39.64 GiB) exactly, with the only differences being the deliberate unit-rendering fix and the aggregates' own observedAt. Resilience to partial input is the substance of this dimension here, and it is handled by refusal rather than by best-effort: a missing, failed or absent step produces an explicit skip or an explicit unpriced audit, never a silently smaller number.

No external API — but there are two internal contracts, and this is the dimension where the new report could most easily rot. First, swamp's WorkflowReportContext: stepExecutions carrying per-step modelType, modelId, dataHandles and status, plus dataRepository.getContent(type, modelId, name, version). Taken from the documented interface and now confirmed live — the report read b2-account's bucket/account snapshots and b2-files' 210 aggregate snapshots from two different models in one execution. Second, the b2-files aggregate shape: bucketName, group (null for the bucket-wide total), listing ('versions' vs 'names'), currentBytes, nonCurrentBytes and truncated. Consumed defensively — every numeric read goes through a finite-number guard that yields null rather than NaN, and an unrecognised shape degrades to 'unmeasured' rather than to zero. Steps are located by the SPECS they wrote, never by step or model name, so renaming a workflow step cannot silently disable the join; asserted by a test that renames both steps and expects identical output.

Read-only and cheap: no B2 transactions, and the reads are bounded by what the workflow already produced (210 aggregates + 47 inventory snapshots on the live run). sizeBucket memoises per subject through joinSizing's cache so a bucket with several findings is sized once. Two substantive judgements sit here. First, the bucket-wide total (group === null) is preferred over summing per-group rows, because the groups are a split OF the total and summing both would double-count; the group sum is a fallback only, and truncation on any group taints it. Second — found LIVE and not by mocking, which is this suite's recurring lesson — a fixed GiB format rendered five buckets as '0.00 GiB' in a worklist whose every row has already passed a > 0 filter, so each of those zeroes was a rounding artefact standing where real data should be: example-delta-ubuntu-v2's 155 bytes and example-gamma-ubuntu's 4.4 MiB read as identically nothing. A report whose entire purpose is refusing to render an unknown as zero must not render a known quantity as zero either. Fixed with scaled units, verified against the same live data (155 B, 2.11 KiB, 4.36 MiB now render), and pinned by test.

Every fixture and README example uses example.com-class names and fake-but-plausible B2 identifiers (example-host-ubuntu, b00000000000000000000001, 0021a2b3c4d5e6f0000000001). Checked with deliberate care this round, because the work involved reading two live fleet reports full of real bucket names and it is exactly the moment one gets pasted into a fixture: the source, the tests and the manifest contain no real bucket name. One correction was made during this review: a first draft of the README quoted its worked worklist using REAL bucket names lifted straight from the live run. Harmless in isolation — they are private-bucket names disclosing no credential or endpoint — but inconsistent with this repo's own standard, which is that published surfaces carry counts and proportions but never real identifiers (the existing README says '0 of 24 buckets', not which 24). Rewritten to example-prefixed names, keeping the real proportions, which is what actually carries the argument. Worth recording because the moment of danger is specific and repeatable: it is while reading live output that a real name gets pasted into a doc.
